item.title: Comment on Future unemployment will be (mostly) voluntary unemployment by Matt2
item.description:
It’s got little to do with being an electrician and a lot to do with being willing to do real remote work - distinct from telework.

$200,000 Australian workers an about $125,000 US. That’s in the same ballpark as Mates on tugs and offshore vessels, jobs that don’t strictly require degrees.

I’m not sure how this can be generalized to “all unemployment will be voluntary.” Not only does the individual worker need to be able to do the job and handle the mental and emotional aspects of regularly dropping in and out of two very different situations (real world/family -vs- the boat, rig, camp) even more importantly their spouse and family have to be able to handle it. It’s not easy. I got lucky and met my wife early. She lived a lot of years with me heading to the office, always with a go bag in the trunk, maybe home that night and maybe getting a call midday that I was airport bound and I’d call when I knew how long I’d be gone. It takes a lot more than technical skills and a decent income to make that life work, but absent the income there’s no reason to even try.

item.title: Comment on Make Sunsets: Geoengineering by Heydocbrowm
item.description:
I know the geoengineering community very well. Make Sunsets is considered dumb cowboys. The challenge with sulfur engineering is not getting it into the atmosphere, it’s understanding its effects because they’re highly regional. If you do it at scale in you’ll overcool that region which will disrupt global weather.

I would suggest looking instead at the Israeli startup Stardust, which has created a molecule that cools but doesn’t cause acid rain and is working diligently at atmospheric modeling.

Silver Linings is a non-profit that funds and advocates for the capacity to do geoengineering effectively.

Alex, I’m happy to make intros for you to these and others, if you’d like to dive deeper into this field.
